messages.subject: General recommendations / integration points
parts:
Hi everyone,

We are trying to use `inlabru` to estimate the population size of a group-living
speciesin a protected area, but we would really appreciate some input, as we are quite new to inlabru etc.

We have counted animals in groups from observations points / plots, with 6
surveys at (most of) each plot, although we pool these surveys together for the
time being. We only observed ~ 110 groups are each survey (513 groups total)
  over a fairly large area, so we'll probably have to stick to simple models.

In addition to modeling the location of groups in space through the SPDE, we
model group size as exponentially distributed, but otherwise 'constant' in space
(ie group size does not depend on the location in space).

Would someone be so kind as to have a look at our script (attached) and let us
know whether we're doing something blatantly wrong ?

In particular, our results have been varying enormously with the mesh and priors
for the Matern correlation structure, as well as with building the integration
points for obtaining the predictions.

We understand such variation based on the mesh etc. is to be expected to some
extent... However, we would really appreciate if someone had recommendations and tips to ensure we have all this set up "correctly" before we move on with this analysis.

Thank you in advance for you valuable help!


Olivier

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] General recommendations / integration points
parts:
Hi,

it's not entirely clear from the code what kind of observation model
you're intending to use, but presumably you are using the actual
_locations_ of points within each plot, so it's a point process model
over the "space-times-size" product domain?
That's at least what the code is setup to do, and I don't see anything
immediately wrong with the structure.

A general observation: Setting a more specific prior distribution on
log.r would likely help, as I expect it to be strongly confounded with
the Intercept. See the development version of inlabru that has a new
feature for converting components into non-Gaussians (via
marginal=bru_mapper_marginal(...)).
With the CRAN version, at least do log.r(1, prec.linear = 1) or
similar, to discourage extreme values.

The predict() step should be insensitive to the integration scheme,
but the modelling step might be more sensitive.
Might be sensible to plot the integration scheme to see what it's doing?

Use
ips <- fm_int(domain = list(size=size_domain,
geometry=geometry_domain), samplers = plots22_sf)
ggplot() + gg(geometry_domain) + geom_sf(data=ips %>% filter(size ==
size_domain$loc[1]), aes(size = weight))

The one part I'm uncertain about is your predict() fm_int construction, with
samplers = list(
size = NULL,
geometry = plots22_sf # 101 survey points
)

Do you get the same integration points if you set
samplers = list(
geometry = plots22_sf # 101 survey points
)
?
Specifically, what happens with "size" in the fm_int() output?
You do need size to be _something_ in the integration points; unclear
if you want to predict for a specific size, or integrate over all of
them.

Finn
